covers.quote: Write the names of individual ships, aircraft and other vehicles:
in italics
with initial capitals.
Separate the names of vehicles from titles in citations and reference lists. Separate them according to the type of publication:
If the title is in italics (such as in book and website titles), use roman type for the name of the vehicle.
If the title is in roman type (such as a journal article), use italics for the name of the vehicle.

examples.note: HMAS Canberra has the specific ship name italicised with initial capital

parts.quote: HMAS Canberra is the Royal Australian Navy’s flagship.

examples.note: Endeavour is italicised and capitalised

parts.quote: Australian–American astronaut Andy Thomas flew his first flight in space aboard the Endeavour.

examples.note: Indian Pacific is italicised and capitalised

parts.quote: The Indian Pacific travels 4,532 kilometres from Perth to Sydney.

examples.note: Tambar in roman type within an italicised book title in a citation

parts.quote: Mair C (2013) The lucky ship: the nine lives of the Australian coaster Tambar1912–1960, Nautical Association of Australia, Australia.

examples.note: Albatross in italics within roman article title in a citation

parts.quote: McMaugh D (21 March 2020) ‘Albatross breaks bread with women in need of a hand’, Navy Daily, accessed 24 March 2020.

rules.quote: Italicise specific names and use capitals
rules.violation_condition: the name of an individual ship, aircraft or other vehicle written without italics or without initial capitals
when: applies to names of individual ships, aircraft and other vehicles
in citations where the publication title is in italics, use roman type instead for the vehicle name

examples.note: Navy ship named without the definite article 'the'

parts.quote: HMAS Canberra is the Royal Australian Navy’s flagship.

rules.quote: Don't use the definite article for navy ships.
rules.violation_condition: the definite article 'the' used before the name of a navy ship (e.g. 'the HMAS Canberra')
rules.why: Distinct naming rule specifically targeting the definite article with navy ships.

covers.quote: Don’t write brands or types of vehicles in italics
Don’t use italics for the ship’s class name.

examples.note: Brand and model capitalised and not italicised

parts.quote: She was driving a Toyota Corolla.

examples.note: Make and model capitalised and not italicised

parts.quote: A Boeing 737 brought the Australians home.

examples.note: Model capitalised and not italicised

parts.quote: They travelled in a Commodore for the last part of the journey.

examples.note: Ship class name 'Anzac Class' capitalised and not italicised

parts.quote: HMASAnzac (III) is the lead ship of eight Anzac Class frigates.

rules.quote: Begin the names of the brands, models and classes of vehicles with an initial capital letter but don’t use italics.
rules.violation_condition: the brand, model, or class of a vehicle written without an initial capital letter or written in italics
when: applies to names of brands, models, and classes of vehicles
rules.why: G-1, G-4: The body sentence e4ef72fdcfb8 gives the complete positive and negative rule covering brand/model/class capitalization and non-italicization.

covers.quote: Use an initial capital for a generic name only if it starts a sentence.

examples.note: Generic vehicle type 'flying boats' in lower case and roman

parts.quote: During the Second World War, flying boats were deployed to strike remote enemy targets to Australia’s north.

examples.note: Generic vehicle type 'biplane' in lower case and roman

parts.quote: The Waco 10 was an open-cockpit biplane introduced in 1927.

examples.note: Generic type 'Mail trains' capitalised only because it begins the sentence

parts.quote: Mail trains stop at every town, adding hours to the trip.

rules.quote: Don’t italicise or capitalise types of ships, aircraft or other vehicles.
rules.violation_condition: a generic type or category of ship, aircraft, or vehicle written with italics or initial capitals (except when starting a sentence)
when: generic vehicle types may be capitalised if they start a sentence
rules.why: G-2: The second sentence states the sentence-initial exception to the general prohibition on capitalising types of vehicles.

examples.note: 'The' is part of the name

parts.quote: The Ghan takes 54 hours to travel from Adelaide to Darwin.

examples.note: 'The' is not part of the name and is not italicised

parts.quote: The Dreamtime was on the shortlist for the name of Qantas’s new fleet of Boeing 787 Dreamliners.

rules.quote: Don’t italicise the definite article (the word ‘the’) before the vehicle’s name unless it is part of the name.
rules.violation_condition: the definite article 'the' preceding a vehicle's name is italicised when it is not part of the proper name
when: does not apply if the definite article is officially part of the vehicle's name
rules.why: Specific, actionable instruction regarding formatting of the definite article before vehicle names.

examples.note: Prefix 'HMAS' is in roman type, while vessel name is italicised

parts.quote: HMAS Arunta, HMAS Sydney

examples.note: Prefix 'PS' is in roman type, while vessel name is italicised

parts.quote: The PS Albury travelled the Murray River in the mid-1800s.

rules.quote: Don’t put the abbreviated parts of a ship’s name in italics.
rules.violation_condition: abbreviations before a ship's name (such as HMAS or PS) written in italics
rules.why: Clear, distinct formatting rule for ship prefix abbreviations.

covers.quote: Use the pronoun ‘it’ for ships, aircraft and other vehicles. Do not write ‘she’ when referring to vehicles in government content. Use pronouns that reflect gender-neutral language.

examples.note: 'its' used instead of 'her'

parts.quote: Brisbane was the first stop for the replica Endeavour on its maiden circumnavigation of Australia.

rules.quote: Refer to vehicles with the pronoun ‘it’
rules.violation_condition: using 'she', 'her', or gendered pronouns rather than 'it' or 'its' to refer to a vehicle
rules.why: G-4: Candidate heading succinctly states the rule; body sentences restate and give rationale.
